intent: Explore a complex domain collaboratively by putting past-tense domain events on a wall in timeline order, so domain experts and developers build one shared behavioural model without a computer in the room.
problem: Domain knowledge is fragmented across people who never meet, so requirements are assembled from partial stories; the mismatches only surface when two teams' models collide in production, and by then the vocabulary that caused the collision has already hardened into code.
context: EventStorming is a workshop format created by Alberto Brandolini in the context of DDD, initially as event-based modelling for teaching DDD building blocks to newcomers. The unit of modelling is a domain event written as a short sentence in a verb at the past tense on an orange sticky note, placed on a paper roll timeline. Deliberately no laptops, no data models, no databases — the constraint is the point, because the value is in the interaction of the people, not in an artefact. The Big Picture variant runs for a whole business line with 15-20 people and is the strongest tool for discovering bounded contexts; a design-level variant later identifies commands, actors, policies and aggregates. Brandolini is explicit that coherence is not the goal of a Big Picture session: the goal is to visualise the current collective understanding, gaps included.
benefits: The domain model is discovered with domain experts present, rather than inferred from their answers later.
Gaps, contradictions and hot spots become visible on the wall while they are still cheap to discuss.
A shared vocabulary emerges naturally, because the events are written in the domain's own words.
The timeline reveals bounded contexts: the language changes at certain points.
Hours of conversation produce an artefact a team can refer back to for months.
tradeoffs: It is a workshop technique, not an implementation pattern: the output is a model, not code.
It needs the right people in the room; a session without a decision-maker produces a model nobody can act on.
It scales badly — a Big Picture workshop for 40 people loses the interaction that makes it work.
The wall is a snapshot; without a follow-up the picture rots and becomes misleading.
Facilitation is a real skill, and a badly facilitated session produces confident nonsense.
Remote facilitation is possible but loses the "everyone talks to everyone" property.
quality_attributes_note: discoverability 10 and simplicity 8 are the point — it is the cheapest way to find out what you do not know. performance/security are not properties of a workshop. testability 4, because the artefact is a model, not a test.

participants.responsibility: Runs the session, manages time and participants, and does not answer domain questions.
participants.notes: Brandolini: full attention means nobody sits down and no laptops.

participants.responsibility: Know the answers; their language is the model's vocabulary.
participants.notes: People who know the questions to ask, and people who know the answers, must both be in the room.

participants.responsibility: Know the questions, and expose where the business flow cannot be implemented.
participants.notes: Brandolini compares it to a walking skeleton: touch every important component as early as possible.

participants.responsibility: A paper roll wide enough that the whole flow is visible at once.
participants.notes: Unlimited modelling surface, usually a long straight wall.

participants.responsibility: A marked unresolved divergence — recorded rather than settled, so exploration continues.
participants.notes: Sometimes a conflict is simply highlighted instead of resolved in the session.

use_cases: Discovering bounded contexts for a whole business line before splitting a monolith.
Aligning a new team on a domain nobody has written down.
Uncovering a contradiction between sales' and operations' understanding of "fulfilled".
Replacing a three-month requirements document with a one-day workshop and a wall.
Onboarding domain experts into an existing codebase by walking its timeline.
avoid_when: You need a specification, not a shared understanding — the artefact is a model, not a contract.
The decision-makers are not in the room; the session produces insight nobody can act on.
The domain is small enough to model in a design session with the actual implementers.
The team wants certainty. A Big Picture deliberately produces a picture of current understanding, including its holes.
Remote-only participation, where the all-to-all interaction the method depends on is hardest to sustain.
pitfalls: Running it with laptops and slides, which turns a modelling workshop into a presentation.
Starting from data or entities instead of events, which produces a data model nobody argues about.
Resolving every conflict on the spot instead of marking hot spots and moving on.
Not narrowing the scope: a whole company on one wall produces a picture nobody can act on.
Leaving with no assigned follow-up, so the picture is never turned into code.
Treating the wall as documentation — it is an artefact for a conversation, not a specification.

related_patterns_notes.bounded-context: The Big Picture recipe is the strongest known technique for discovering bounded contexts: the language changes at certain points on the timeline.
related_patterns_notes.ubiquitous-language: Every event is a sentence in the domain's own words, so the workshop is a language-discovery mechanism.
related_patterns_notes.domain-event: The event is the modelling unit — a past-tense statement of a state transition the business cares about.
related_patterns_notes.aggregate: At design level, the workshop identifies the aggregates within which commands produce events.

anti_patterns: Using EventStorming as the specification for an implementation team.
Letting the facilitator answer domain questions instead of making the group answer them.
Starting with commands or aggregates rather than events.
Running it as a one-off and never returning to the picture as the model evolves.
design_principles: EventStorming is a workshop-based method to quickly find out what is happening in the domain of a software program; it is extremely lightweight and intentionally requires no support by a computer (Wikipedia).
The result is expressed in sticky notes on a wide wall; the business process is stormed out as a series of domain events denoted by orange stickies.
A domain event is written as a short sentence using a verb at the past tense (Brandolini).
It is essential to have the right people present: those who know the questions to ask (typically developers) and those who know the answers (domain experts, product owners).
The Big Picture structure is chaotic exploration, then enforcing the timeline, then people and systems, then problems and opportunities, then picking a problem.
In a Big Picture workshop, coherence is not the goal — visualising the current state of understanding, gaps included, is.
best_practices: Bring the people who know the questions and the people who know the answers, in the same room.
Narrow the scope before you start; decide which process you are storming, not the whole company.
No laptops, no slides — the artefact is sticky notes on a wall.
Write every event as a verb in the past tense, in the language the business actually uses.
Mark hot spots and move on; a session that resolves everything resolves nothing.
Finish by converting the picture into something real — bounded contexts, a domain model, an aggregate list — or it will not survive.
